titre: Why leaves turn red in autumn remains an open question
accroche: Autumn yellow is chlorophyll withdrawing. Red, on the other hand, is made on purpose, at a real cost, and no one really knows why.
contenu_vulgarise:
Every autumn, leaves turn yellow because chlorophyll, which masked the other pigments all year long, breaks down and lets carotenoids and xanthophylls show through, which have been there since spring. This mechanism is well understood and costs the tree almost nothing: the yellow pigments were already present, and the leaf simply stops hiding them.

Red does not work that way. The anthocyanin that colors many species red, red maple, dogwood, sumac, does not exist in the green leaf of summer: the tree makes it from scratch at the very moment it is getting ready to lose the leaf, investing sugar and energy in it. A study of eighty-nine tree species at the Harvard Forest finds that 70% of them synthesize anthocyanin in autumn. The question this figure raises is simple: why spend a resource on a leaf that is going to fall anyway?

## Two Hypotheses, and Neither Prevails

The first, photoprotection, proposes that anthocyanin acts as a screen, limiting the light that reaches a chlorophyll in the process of breaking down, in order to protect the recovery of nitrogen before the leaf falls. The Harvard Forest study, however, finds a weak correlation between anthocyanin content and the efficiency of that recovery, which the authors themselves describe as tenuous evidence.

The second hypothesis, put forward by the biologist William Hamilton in 2001, is more surprising: red would be a costly signal addressed to the aphids that choose their host tree in autumn, a way for the tree to advertise its defenses and discourage the most demanding insects. The idea has been tested directly: in 2005, German researchers painted half the trees in a population of rowans red, and left the others green, to isolate the effect of color alone. The number of aphids trapped on the painted branches does not differ from that on the green ones; it is the quantity of fruit the tree bears, not its color, that predicts infestation.

## What This Shifts

The two best-documented hypotheses have each been undermined by the very data meant to confirm them. It remains possible that anthocyanin serves yet another purpose, or that it does a little of all this without any one effect dominating enough to show up in an experiment. For a pigment that millions of people photograph every autumn, the explanation for its very existence remains, for now, without a firm answer.

repere.texte: Of 89 tree species examined at the Harvard Forest, 70% (62 of 89) synthesize anthocyanin in autumn, but anthocyanin content is only weakly correlated with the efficiency of nitrogen recovery before leaf fall, the authors themselves speaking of tenuous evidence.
repere.source: Lee, Lee, O'Keefe, Holbrook & Feild, “Pigment dynamics and autumn leaf senescence in a New England deciduous forest, eastern USA,” Ecological Research, 18, 2003

carte.punch: Autumn red costs the tree sugar. No one really knows what it is for.
carte.idee: Autumn yellow is just chlorophyll withdrawing and revealing pigments that were already there. Red is made on purpose by the tree just before the leaf falls. Two hypotheses about its purpose, protection and a signal to aphids, have each been undermined by the data.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The original costly-signal hypothesis addressed to aphids, with the data comparing tree species.

quiz.question: Why does the red coloring of autumn leaves raise a different question from the yellow coloring?
choix: Because red fades faster than yellow once the leaf has fallen
Because yellow appears only on cultivated trees, never in the wild
Because the tree makes red by spending energy, whereas yellow was already present
Because only red attracts pollinators in autumn
quiz.explication: Yellow comes from the unmasking of pigments (carotenoids, xanthophylls) already present all year in the green leaf, at no notable cost. Red, from anthocyanin, is synthesized from scratch just before the leaf falls, which raises the question of its usefulness since it costs a resource to an organ about to drop.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the study carried out at the Harvard Forest, what proportion of the 89 tree species examined synthesize anthocyanin in autumn?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The study by Lee et al. (2003) at Harvard Forest finds that 62 species out of 89, or 70%, synthesize anthocyanin de novo at the time of senescence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the 2005 experiment show, in which German researchers colored red half the branches of a population of rowans?
choix: The branches painted red attracted significantly more aphids than the green ones
No aphids were observed on the painted branches, whatever the color
The number of aphids trapped does not depend on color, but on the quantity of fruit the tree bears
The aphids avoided both the red and the green branches in favor of the unpainted ones
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The number of aphids trapped does not differ between red and green branches; it is the quantity of fruit the tree bears that predicts infestation, not its color.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the photoprotection hypothesis, what would the red anthocyanin made just before the leaf falls be for?
choix: To attract pollinating insects before winter
To replace the vanished chlorophyll so that photosynthesis can continue
To keep frost from destroying the leaf's cells
To screen out light in order to protect nitrogen recovery before the leaf falls
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The photoprotection hypothesis proposes that anthocyanin limits the light reaching a chlorophyll that is breaking down, in order to protect the recovery of nitrogen.
